record_reviews.summary: Erasmus supplies a compact geometric calculation for the obtuse angle of a dodecahedron, relating its height to the hexagon side in a bee cell and giving the numerical result 0.088 (P1). The fragment is an incoming technical answer, but no specific Darwin question is preserved in this packet and the calculation cannot be assigned to the later basin work.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From Erasmus Alvey Darwin [May–June 1858]1

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus works through the dodecahedron geometry step by step: sphere and hexagon radii, the 0.028-inch difference, distances to obtuse and acute angles, and a final ¾ of 1/100 inch (P1–12). He invites further questions because explanations save Darwin trouble (P13), and an enclosure preserves his geometric construction. This is a technical incoming calculation with its own enclosure layer, not a Darwin-authored result.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin [before 8 June 1858]1

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus sends additional projections, rhombs, a pyramid and instructions for assembling a dodecahedron model, saying the model will clarify the positions of the acute and obtuse angles (P1–10). The later blocks label equator, meridian and east–west circles and count six acute and eight obtuse angles (P11–16); the enclosures contain separate projection diagrams. The source answers an unlocated geometry exchange, but no Darwin outgoing prompt is available here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin [8 June 1858]1

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus sends a model and says that turning the triangles and semicircles perpendicular makes a quarter of a dodecahedron, then dismisses it as a Chinese puzzle (P1–2). Its XML bound extends after 8 June 1858 through 1882, so the supplied 'after 8 June' label does not establish a precise composition or receipt day.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin [after 8 June 1858]1

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus returns a bee-cell basin diagram with dimensions and explains projections of intersecting spheres, including why three spheres cannot be drawn together at real dimensions (P1–3). He compares a potato slice at latitude 45° with a sphere intersection and remarks that Darwin has carriage and horses trouble as well as bee-cell trouble (P4–5). The two enclosures add measured/foreshortened dimensions and Darwin's own corrections; they remain visual and marginal layers, not a new body prompt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin [19 June 1858]1

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus's record is incomplete: the surviving opening recommends Bucknill's Psychology of Shakespeare from the London Library, explains that its psychology is restricted to mental disease, and stops mid-sentence (P1). The later-bound date '[1859 or later]' and catalogue publication note do not prove a complete 1859 letter or Darwin receipt; no relationship is proposed.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin 15 August [1859 or later]1Aug 15th

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus reports Henry Holland's partial and conflicted reading of Origin: Holland has read only about half, finds the eye and ear arguments difficult, and has withdrawn an article that would have had to engage Darwin's book (P1). Erasmus then gives her own enthusiastic response, especially to geographical distribution and island/continent relations (P3), clearly separating Holland's reported voice from hers. This is second-hand knowledge delivered to Darwin, not a Holland-to-Darwin letter or direct answer to a Darwin prompt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin 23 November [1859]1Nov 23

record_reviews.summary: Darwin corrects Phillips's apparent advertisement as president of the Zoological Section at Leeds, saying he had never heard of it and cannot attend because of health and other circumstances (P1–3). The body is administrative correction; the source does not preserve the Phillips notice or establish what Phillips had written.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To John Phillips 1 September [1858]1Down Bromley KentSept. 1

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Phillips that Murray will send the condensed Origin, asks him to read it straight through, and explains that he hopes Phillips may see more evidence for mutability despite his opposing view (P1–2). He identifies Hooker as a leading judge and says the note needs no answer (P3). Phillips's acknowledgment is missing, so no incoming reply is established here.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Phillips for his note and asks him to judge whether natural selection can explain island affinities, oceanic-island inhabitants, classification, morphology, embryology and rudimentary organs (P1). He acknowledges that palaeontology and his explanations may be opposed or fallacious, then calls the book his offspring (P2–3). The preceding Phillips note is missing; this is a later defence, not a reconstructed reply pair.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Phillips for a full note that sent him back to Lardner's Encyclopaedia and sets out his coast-ice/subsiding-land explanation for erratic boulders (P1). He asks whether upper conglomerate boulders at 700–900 feet are rounded or angular (P2), while distinguishing this narrow question from the general erratics problem; the presumed Phillips note is absent from the packet.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin returns repeatedly to the erratic-boulder issue and describes De la Beche's alternative denudation theory (P1–4). He asks Phillips for one authoritative sentence and whether the red conglomerate strata are gently inclined, while accepting that Phillips may not reply before the paper is read (P5–8). The XML alternatives are 7 or 14 April 1848; the letter's paper deadline bounds timing but does not choose one date.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Erasmus to place Anne's death announcement in the Times and other large-circulation papers, offering to pay for the notices and telegraph (P1–3). He describes Emma's grief and Fanny's comfort at Malvern (P4–6). This is a private/logistical outgoing letter whose same-day incoming response is 1418, not a scientific prompt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To E. A. Darwin [25 April 1851]Down.Friday

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus writes after Darwin's return from Malvern, expressing concern for Charles and Emma and describing Anne's death as an inexpressible loss (P1–2). The Friday-night body is an emotional same-day response to 1416's death-notice and family update; it does not address the newspaper mechanics in detail.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin [25 April 1851]Friday Night

record_reviews.summary: Darwin reports Josiah's second letter about the £5000 trust, plans a share transfer, sends a trust-property list and discusses a large tank/siphon scheme (P1–3). His postscript asks Erasmus to acknowledge the trust documents and return an enclosed declaration, distinguishing financial documents from the water-work question (P4). Erasmus's same-day acknowledgment is 1516.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To E. A. Darwin 26 [April 1853]Down.26th.

record_reviews.summary: Erasmus acknowledges receipt of Darwin's trust statement and lists securities held, including the marriage settlement, Muckleston mortgage and Major Owens mortgage, while noting two railway shares not yet received (P1–11). The source is a custody/accounting acknowledgment, not an endorsement of Darwin's legal interpretation; it directly answers 1380's document request on 26 April 1853.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From E. A. Darwin 26 April 1853April 26 1853

record_reviews.summary: Darwin urges Phillips to read his earlier chapter on cleavage and foliation, citing specific pages, observations from Chile and the Chonos Group, and the distinction between cleavage, stratification and foliation (P1–3). He then asks whether pressure could break and recement clay-slate/grauwacke like glacier ice (P6–7), offers copies of the three volumes (P8–9), and supplies no identified Phillips prompt.
